questions.q: How does k-nearest neighbors make a classification for a new row?
options: It fits a line through the training data and reads off the class
It finds the k closest training rows and lets them vote
It multiplies class probabilities under an independence assumption
It builds a tree of yes/no questions during training
questions.explain: k-NN stores the training rows and, at prediction time, takes a vote among the k nearest ones.

questions.q: In the lesson, unscaled k-NN scored 0.453 and scaled k-NN scored 0.9. What explains the difference?
options: Scaling adds more training rows
Scaling changes the value of k
A feature on a huge scale dominated the distance calculation until it was standardized
Scaling removes the need for a test set
questions.explain: k-NN relies on distance, so a feature measured in the thousands drowns out small-scale features unless features are scaled.

questions.q: With k = 1, the scaled model scored 1.000 on training data and 0.900 on test data. What does that gap suggest?
options: Overfitting: the model chases noise in the training rows
Underfitting: the model is too simple
Data leakage from the test set
The model needs more features
questions.explain: A perfect training score with a noticeably lower test score is the classic overfit pattern, and k = 1 is the most flexible setting.

questions.q: What is the 'naive' assumption in naive Bayes?
options: All classes are equally likely
Features are independent of each other given the class
The data has no missing values
The training set is larger than the test set
questions.explain: Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class. It is rarely exactly true, but it makes training fast and simple.

questions.q: Which situation is naive Bayes a well-known good fit for?
options: Predicting house prices from a handful of continuous features
Text classification such as spam filtering using word counts
Finding customer segments without labels
Reducing 100 features down to 2
questions.explain: MultinomialNB works on count features like word frequencies, which is why it is a classic choice for spam and text classification.
